laws: Land Ordinance
The first survey law holds back one third of any gold, silver, lead and copper mines for Congress to dispose of.
Lead mines leased
Lead mines on the public lands are reserved from sale and may be leased.
Mineral lands put on sale
Acts of 1846 and 1847 open the reserved lead and copper lands of the upper Mississippi and Lake Superior to sale.
Lode Mining Act
The mineral lands of the public domain are declared free and open to exploration, and lode claims may be patented.
Placer Act
Placer claims may be patented.
General Mining Law
A valid mining claim may be patented, surface and minerals together. Mineral land stays closed to farm entry.
Coal Lands Act
Coal land is sold by the acre at a set minimum price, in limited amounts to each buyer.
Coal withdrawals
Tens of millions of acres of western coal land are withdrawn from entry while the Geological Survey classes them.
First coal reservation
Act of 3 March: a settler on land later classed as coal land may take a patent to the surface, with the coal kept by the United States.
Coal lands opened to farm entry
Act of 22 June: withdrawn and classified coal land may be entered for farming, the coal reserved. The Pickett Act of 25 June confirms the President's power to withdraw land.
Oil, gas, phosphate and potash reserved
Act of 17 July: land withdrawn or classed for phosphate, nitrate, potash, oil, gas or asphaltic minerals may be entered, with those minerals reserved.
Stock-Raising Homestead Act
640-acre grazing homesteads, each patent reserving all the coal and other minerals to the United States, with a right to enter and mine.
Mineral Leasing Act
Coal, oil, gas, phosphate, sodium and oil shale on public land, including the reserved minerals, are leased for a royalty and no longer sold.
Taylor Grazing Act
Most of the remaining public domain is closed to entry. Its exchanges with states and private owners may keep the minerals on either side.
Bankhead-Jones Act
Failed farm land is bought back. Many sellers, or owners before them, keep the minerals.
Small Tract Act
Five-acre tracts for homes and cabins, with oil, gas and other minerals reserved.
Acquired lands leasing
Minerals under land the United States bought are brought under leasing.
Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act
Village corporations receive the surface of their selections; twelve regional corporations receive the subsurface.
Federal Land Policy and Management Act
Homesteading ends in the lower 48. Section 209 keeps all minerals in federal hands when land is conveyed, with narrow exceptions.
Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act
Federal coal under a private surface may not be strip-mined without the surface owner's written consent.
Watt v. Western Nuclear
The Supreme Court holds that gravel is among the minerals reserved by a stock-raising homestead patent.
Amoco v. Southern Ute Tribe
The Supreme Court holds that the coal reserved under the 1909 and 1910 acts does not include the gas held in it.
